title: Tribal council 'devastated' after RCMP cleared in fatal shooting
article: The Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council says it is devastated that the province's civilian-led police watchdog has cleared RCMP officers in the fatal shooting of a First Nations man last year on a reserve near Tofino.

"It is disillusioning and frustrating that once again an RCMP officer killed a First Nation person without consequences," the council said in a statement Thursday. "There is always hope that justice will happen for our First Nations people who lose their life in these circumstances."
Julian Jones, 28, a Tla-o-qui-aht member, was killed by RCMP on Feb. 27, 2021, in the Tla-o-qui-aht community of Opitsaht on Meares Island.

The Independent Investigations Office of B.C. said Tofino RCMP officers responded to a report of a woman being held against her will at a residence. Jones was shot and killed by police and another man was taken into custody during the incident.

The IIO said this week its investigation had cleared the officers, but further details and the rationale behind its decision could not be released because a matter related to the shooting is before the courts.

"I regret that the frustration this lack of information will cause is required to ensure a fair trial," said IIO chief civilian director Ronald MacDonald. "However, I feel it necessary to advise the public, and in particular the family of the deceased and other involved parties, that this investigation has concluded in as timely a manner as possible."
He said once the court process concludes, the IIO will meet with family and community members to review the investigation and answer questions.
The Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council said the shooting was a shock to the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation and all Nuu-chah-nulth Nations and peoples.

"The news that there will be no charges is further devastating and hurtful to the family, community and Nation. There is always hope that the system will bring justice for a person killed by police, but the reality never lives up to this hope as the system is stacked against us," the council said in a statement.

In April, an Indigenous civilian monitor was appointed to look over a report by the IIO following the Meares Island shooting - the first time a First Nations monitor has been appointed in such a case and considered a step in building trust, according to the IIO.
The IIO said the nation's chief, Thomas George, would receive "unfettered access to all of its investigative materials."

The IIO said this week that MacDonald had reviewed the final report of the Indigenous civilian monitor and all available evidence - including information from witnesses and forensic scene analysis - and determined that there are no reasonable grounds to believe that any officer committed an offence.
The matter will not be referred to Crown Counsel for consideration of charges, and the investigation is concluded, the IIO said.
The IIO's public report and the final report of the Indigenous civilian monitor are expected to be published on the IIO website when the court process has concluded.

Jones' shooting was the second police shooting of a Tla-o-qui-aht member in nine months. Chantel Moore was fatally shot on June 4, 2020 in New Brunswick by an Edmundston police officer, who was also cleared by civilian police investigators.
Judith Sayers, president of the Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council, said frustration is mounting.

Sayers said RCMP and other police forces should all wear body cameras and need to train their officers to disarm and de-escalate situations so shootings aren't necessary. She wants the IIO to be more "reflective and inclusive" of First Nations in their investigations.
And Sayers wants an alternate system to 911 for wellness checks, where trauma professionals are initial responders instead of police.
The Opitsaht community is part of the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation, a member of the Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council, which has more than 10,000 members.
